```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 5.2, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

A survey that measures several constructs with several items each poses two
questions at once: how the respondents answered each item, and how the items
relate to the construct they are meant to measure. The usual displays answer
one question at a time. A stacked bar chart of 34 items shows the response
distributions but not which items belong together or move together; a
correlation matrix shows the associations but not the distributions. A snake
plot with one panel per construct keeps the items of a construct together,
orders them by their level of endorsement, and can print the correlation
between neighbouring items at the U-turn that joins them.

This case study describes a 34-item student survey with four constructs. It
first gives an overview of all constructs, then asks which engagement items
are most and least endorsed and whether the ordering criterion matters, where
the mean and the median of an item part ways, and which engagement items vary
together across students. The plots are drawn with `survey_snake()`; the
numbers behind them are computed alongside.

```{r package}
library(snakeplot)
```

## Data

`student_survey` holds the person-level scores of 280 university students from
an experience sampling study (Neubauer & Schmiedek, 2024; data CC-BY 4.0 at
<https://osf.io/bhq3p>). Each score is the student's mean over the study,
rounded to a 1–5 scale (rescaled from the original 1–7). The column names
carry the construct as a prefix:

- **Respondent:** one row per student.
- **Emotions:** `Emo_` — 10 items, such as `Emo_Happy` and `Emo_Worried`.
- **Study motivation:** `Mot_` — 8 items, such as `Mot_Interesting` and
  `Mot_Compulsory`.
- **Emotion regulation:** `Reg_` — 5 items, such as `Reg_Rumination` and
  `Reg_Suppression`.
- **Study engagement:** `Eng_` — 11 items, such as `Eng_Enjoy` and
  `Eng_ConsiderQuitting`.

```{r data}
dim(student_survey)
table(construct = sub("_.*", "", names(student_survey)))
scale_labels <- c("1" = "1 (low)", "2" = "2", "3" = "3", "4" = "4",
                  "5" = "5 (high)")
```

The data hold 280 students and 34 items: 10 emotion, 11 engagement, 8
motivation and 5 regulation items. The items are named by their content
(for example `Eng_ConsiderQuitting`); the wording of each item is in the
original study's codebook, so the interpretation below stays with the item
names.

The summary table below gives, for every item, its construct, mean, median and
net score (the share of responses above the scale midpoint of 3 minus the
share below it). It is the numerical counterpart of the plots that follow.

```{r item-summary}
item_summary <- data.frame(
  construct = sub("_.*", "", names(student_survey)),
  item      = sub("^(Emo|Mot|Reg|Eng)_", "", names(student_survey)),
  mean      = colMeans(student_survey),
  median    = vapply(student_survey, median, numeric(1)),
  net       = colMeans(student_survey > 3) - colMeans(student_survey < 3),
  row.names = NULL
)
sort_by(item_summary, ~ construct + mean)
```

## An overview of the four constructs

The first question is how the four constructs compare: which have items with
high endorsement, and how spread out are the item means within a construct?
The range of item means per construct:

```{r construct-range}
aggregate(mean ~ construct, data = item_summary, FUN = range)
```

The emotion items have the widest range of means, from 1.37 (`Angry`) to
3.55 (`Happy`): the construct mixes rarely felt negative emotions with
commonly felt positive ones. The motivation items range from 2.11 to 3.86 and
the engagement items from 1.71 to 3.41. The regulation items have the
narrowest range, from 2.24 to 3.32.

With `facet = TRUE`, `survey_snake()` groups the columns by the prefix before
the underscore, draws one panel per group, and removes the prefix from the
item labels. `sort_by = "mean"` orders the items of each panel by ascending
mean, so every panel runs from its least to its most endorsed item.

```{r facet, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 7.5}
survey_snake(student_survey, facet = TRUE, facet_ncol = 2L,
             tick_shape = "bar", sort_by = "mean",
             colors = snake_palette("earth", n = 5),
             level_labels = scale_labels)
```

Each band is one item, drawn as a stacked bar of the percentage of students
at each level, with the percentage written in segments wide enough to hold
it; the diamond marks the item mean. The first band of each panel is the
item with the lowest mean in the table above (`Angry`, `Disappointed`,
`Suppression`, `ConsiderQuitting`) and the last band the item with the
highest (`Happy`, `FeltBad`, `FocusGood`, `OnlyNecessary`).

## Which engagement items are endorsed most and least?

The engagement construct has the most items (11), and the following
questions use it. The items sorted by mean, with the net score alongside:

```{r engagement-order}
engagement <- subset(student_survey, select = Eng_Enjoy:Eng_ConsiderQuitting)
sort_by(subset(item_summary, construct == "Eng"), ~ mean)
```

`ConsiderQuitting` has by far the lowest mean (1.71) and net score (−0.736):
far more students are below the midpoint than above it.
`DifficultReconcile` (2.51), `WearingDown` (2.65) and `Energy` (2.67)
follow. At the top are `OnlyNecessary` (3.41), `Satisfied` (3.34) and `Enjoy`
(3.19). The net score increases in the same order as the mean, so for these
items `sort_by = "net"` and `sort_by = "mean"` produce the same bands; the
closest pair, `WearingDown` and `Energy`, differs by 0.004 in net score
(−0.293 against −0.289). The two criteria can only disagree for items whose
means are close, as the emotion items `Afraid` and `Sad` do in
[the palettes and layout guide](palettes-and-layout.html).

## Where do the mean and the median part ways?

An item mean is a fair summary of a symmetric distribution but not of a
skewed one. The question is which items have a median at least half a scale
point away from their mean:

```{r mean-median}
subset(item_summary, abs(mean - median) >= 0.5)
```

Eleven items meet the criterion. In seven of them the median of 4 lies above
the mean (for example `Satisfied`, mean 3.34, and `OnlyNecessary`, mean
3.41): the typical student answers 4, and the mean is pulled down by students
at the lower levels. In the other four, all engagement items, the median lies
below the mean: `DifficultReconcile`, `WearingDown` and `Energy` have a
median of 2 and means between 2.51 and 2.67, and `ConsiderQuitting` has a
median of 1 and a mean of 1.71. For these items the typical student is at the
low end and the mean is pulled up by a minority at the higher levels. Six of
the eleven items belong to the engagement construct.

`show_median = TRUE` adds a vertical line at the item median to the mean
diamond. On the engagement items:

```{r markers}
survey_snake(engagement, tick_shape = "bar", sort_by = "mean",
             show_mean = TRUE, show_median = TRUE,
             colors = snake_palette("earth", n = 5),
             level_labels = scale_labels,
             title = "Engagement: mean (diamond) and median (line)")
```

The diamond marks the mean and the dashed line the median of each item. Both
markers are placed on the response scale, which runs from level 1 at the left
end of the band to level 5 at the right end, so one scale point is a quarter of
the band width; they are not tied to the stacked segments, whose widths are
percentages. The horizontal distance between the two markers is therefore the
difference between mean and median: 0.71 scale points for
`ConsiderQuitting`, between 0.5 and 0.7 for the other five engagement items in
the table above, and less than half a point for the remaining five. A reader
who sees only the diamond on `ConsiderQuitting` would place the typical
student between levels 1 and 2; the median places that student at level 1.

## Which engagement items vary together?

The last question concerns associations: do students who endorse one
engagement item also endorse its neighbour? `arc_fill = "correlation"`
computes the Pearson correlation between each pair of adjacent items across
the students who answered both, prints it at the U-turn that joins them, and
tints the arc by its sign (`arc_color` for positive, its complement for
negative) and strength. Because the correlation pairs each student's answer
to one item with the same student's answer to the next, it needs the raw
responses, one row per student; `survey_snake()` refuses a table of counts
for this fill. The plot returns its layout invisibly, and the correlations it
printed are returned by `as.data.frame()` with `what = "correlations"`.

```{r correlation}
engagement_layout <- survey_snake(engagement, tick_shape = "line",
                                  arc_fill = "correlation", sort_by = "mean",
                                  colors = snake_palette("earth", n = 5),
                                  level_labels = scale_labels,
                                  title = "Engagement: correlations at U-turns")
as.data.frame(engagement_layout, what = "correlations")
```

Each band is one item, sorted by mean, with one tick per student in the zone
of the student's response level; the number at each U-turn is the
correlation `r` between the two items it joins, computed over `n` students.
All ten correlations use the 280 students. The upper half of the order forms
a strongly correlated chain: `Expectations`, `Identification`, `Interesting`,
`Enjoy` and `Satisfied` correlate between 0.78 and 0.81 with their
neighbours. Two U-turns carry negative correlations, `Exhausted` with
`Expectations` (−0.293) and `Satisfied` with `OnlyNecessary` (−0.205), and
the arcs there take the complementary tint. The weakest positive links are
`WearingDown` with `Energy` (0.153) and `Energy` with `Exhausted` (0.194).

The arcs report only adjacent pairs, and the order by mean is not chosen to
place related items next to each other. `WearingDown` and `Exhausted` are
separated by `Energy` in this order; their correlation, computed directly:

```{r non-adjacent}
with(student_survey, cor(Eng_WearingDown, Eng_Exhausted))
```

At 0.72 it is far stronger than either of their correlations with `Energy`,
which sits between them only because its mean (2.67) falls between theirs
(2.65 and 2.80). A weak arc therefore means that two neighbouring items are
weakly related, not that an item is unrelated to the rest of its construct.

## Conclusions

- The four constructs differ in spread: emotion item means range from 1.37
  to 3.55, regulation item means only from 2.24 to 3.32.
- `ConsiderQuitting` is the least endorsed engagement item (mean 1.71, net
  score −0.736); `OnlyNecessary` and `Satisfied` are the most endorsed.
- For the engagement items, sorting by mean and by net score gives the same
  order.
- Eleven of the 34 items have a median at least half a point from the mean;
  in seven the median is higher, in four engagement items, among them
  `ConsiderQuitting`, it is lower. `show_median = TRUE` draws the gap in the
  plot.
- The engagement items `Expectations`, `Identification`, `Interesting`,
  `Enjoy` and `Satisfied` form a chain of correlations between 0.78 and 0.81;
  `Exhausted`–`Expectations` and `Satisfied`–`OnlyNecessary` are negatively
  correlated. Correlation arcs show only neighbours in the chosen order, so a
  weak arc calls for a direct check, as for `WearingDown` and `Exhausted`
  (r = 0.72).

The daily, beep-level counterpart of the emotion items is analysed in
[the daily emotions case study](case-daily-emotions.html); colour and
ordering choices are discussed in
[the palettes and layout guide](palettes-and-layout.html).

## Reference

Neubauer, A. B., & Schmiedek, F. (2024). Approaching academic adjustment on

147–168. <https://doi.org/10.1007/s11618-023-01182-8>
